cards.front: Bull vs. Bear
cards.back: Bull: believes a market or security will rise in value (bullish). Bear: believes a market or security will fall in value (bearish). A short seller is considered a bear.

cards.front: What are the components of a typical two-sided stock quote?
cards.back: Bid (highest price a buyer will pay), Ask/Offer (lowest price a seller will accept), and Size (shares available at each side, expressed in round lots of 100). The bid is always lower than the ask.

cards.front: BCO stock is quoted: Bid 42 – Ask 42.50, size 10 x 12. A customer enters a market order to buy 500 shares. At what price will the order execute, and how many shares are available at that price?
cards.back: The customer buys at the ask = $42.50. Up to 1,200 shares (12 × 100) are available at $42.50. The 500-share order fills at $42.50.

cards.front: On an exchange, how does the DMM's order book determine the bid and ask?
cards.back: The highest open buy limit order establishes the bid (and its size); the lowest open sell limit order establishes the ask (and its size).

cards.front: In the OTC market, how are the bid and ask determined when multiple market makers quote a stock?
cards.back: The inside quote is the highest bid among all market makers and the lowest ask among all market makers. The customer sells to a dealer at the bid and buys from a dealer at the ask.

cards.front: Spread
cards.back: The difference between the bid and ask prices. Represents the market maker's potential profit (buys at bid, sells at ask). The highest bid/lowest ask combination is called the inside market or inside quote.

cards.front: ABC stock is quoted 25.20 bid – 25.22 ask, size 5 x 12. What is the spread?
What is the minimum price increment for stock quotes priced above $1.00?
cards.back: One cent ($0.01). Sub-penny pricing is permitted only for stocks trading below $1.00.

cards.front: Market order
cards.back: An order to buy or sell that is executed immediately at the best available market price. Market orders take precedence over limit orders.

cards.front: Limit order
cards.back: An order with a specified price: the maximum price a buyer will pay (buy limit) or the minimum price a seller will accept (sell limit). May be executed at the limit price or better; risk is missing the market if the price is never reached.

cards.front: For a buy limit and a sell limit, what does "or better" mean?
cards.back: Buy limit: "or better" = at the limit price or LOWER. Sell limit: "or better" = at the limit price or HIGHER.

cards.front: ABC is trading at $63. Julia Miller wants to buy ABC only if its price falls to $58 or lower. Which order type should she place?
cards.back: A buy limit order at $58. The order will execute only at $58 or lower (better for a buyer).

cards.front: Stop order
cards.back: Not a live order, but a trigger. When the stock trades at or through the stop price, the stop order becomes a market order and is executed immediately at the best available price. Stop orders have no time-priority standing.

cards.front: Stop-limit order
cards.back: When the stop price is reached, the order becomes a limit order (not a market order). It may or may not execute, depending on whether the market reaches the limit price.

cards.front: BCO is trading at $12. A customer enters: Buy 2,000 BCO at 15 stop limit 16. Explain how this order works.
cards.back: When BCO trades at or through $15 (the stop), the order is triggered and becomes a buy limit at $16. It will execute only if BCO can be purchased at $16 or lower.

cards.front: Day order
cards.back: Default time restriction. Valid only until the close of trading on the day entered. Any unexecuted portion is canceled at day's end.

cards.front: Good-til-canceled (GTC) order
cards.back: Valid until executed or canceled. Automatically canceled if unexecuted on the last business day of April and the last business day of October unless the customer renews it.

cards.front: Fill-or-kill (FOK) order
cards.back: Must be executed in its entirety immediately, or the entire order is canceled. No partial fills allowed.

cards.front: Immediate-or-cancel (IOC) order
cards.back: Execute as much as possible immediately; cancel any unfilled portion. Partial fills ARE allowed (unlike FOK).

cards.front: All-or-none (AON) order
cards.back: Must be filled in its entirety, but does NOT need to be filled immediately. May be a day or GTC order. No partial fills allowed.

cards.front: Long position: how is it opened and closed, and what is the maximum loss?
cards.back: Buy to open, sell to close. The investor is bullish. Maximum loss equals the cost basis (if the security becomes worthless).

cards.front: Short position: how is it opened and closed, and what is the loss potential?
cards.back: Sell to open (borrowed shares), buy to close (cover). The investor is bearish. Loss potential is UNLIMITED because there is no cap on how high the stock can rise.

cards.front: A customer shorts 3,000 shares of XYZ at $30 and later covers at $24. What is the result?
cards.back: Profit of $6 per share × 3,000 shares = $18,000. The short was closed (covered) by buying back at a lower price than the short sale price.

cards.front: Differentiate a broker-dealer acting in an agency capacity vs. a principal capacity.
cards.back: Agency (broker): trades on behalf of customers with another party; charges a commission. Principal (dealer/market maker): trades with the customer from the firm's own inventory; profits on the markup/markdown (spread). A BD may act as both, but not in both capacities on the same transaction.

cards.front: What is regular-way settlement for corporate stocks and bonds, municipal bonds, and agency/GSE securities?
cards.back: T+1 — settlement by the end of the first business day after the trade date (effective 5/28/2024).

cards.front: What is regular-way settlement for U.S. Treasury securities (T-bills, T-notes, T-bonds) and options?
cards.back: T+1 — the next business day after trade date.

cards.front: Cash settlement
cards.back: Same-day settlement: delivery of securities and payment occur on the trade date. Both buyer and seller must agree to cash settlement BEFORE the trade takes place. (Not to be confused with a "cash trade," which simply means paid in full without margin.)

cards.front: Bao Chiang buys 100 shares of ABC common stock on Thursday, June 30. By when must cash be in her account to pay for the trade? (July 4 is a holiday.)
cards.back: Regular-way settlement for corporate stock is T+1. One business day after Thursday June 30 is Friday, July 1. Cash must be available by the close of business on Friday, July 1.

cards.front: When an equity option is exercised, when does the resulting stock transaction settle?
cards.back: T+1 — the second business day after exercise was T+2 under the old rules, but effective 5/28/2024, equity option exercises settle T+1, aligned with regular-way equity settlement.

cards.front: When an index option is exercised, how and when is settlement made?
cards.back: Cash settlement only — the writer pays the holder the intrinsic value in cash on the next business day (T+1). There is no underlying security to deliver.

cards.front: What are the requirements for "good delivery" of a physical stock certificate?
cards.back: The certificate must be (1) endorsed/signed by all owners listed on its face, and (2) signed exactly as the name appears. Permitted substitutions include "&" for "and," "Co." for "Company," and "Inc." for "Incorporated."

cards.front: Stock power (bond power)
cards.back: A separate signed document used in place of endorsing the back of a certificate. Identifies the specific certificate (issuer, share count, certificate number). Commonly used when certificates are mailed, so the unsigned certificate and the power can be sent separately for security.

cards.front: Street name (book-entry)
cards.back: Securities held electronically by a broker-dealer on behalf of the customer. No physical certificate exists and no physical signature is needed for good delivery. U.S. Treasuries, for example, are issued only in book-entry form.
